title: Market Structures, Integration, Consolidation and the Distribution of Control

paras: A comparative framework for monopoly, oligopoly, vertical and horizontal integration, and the changing balance of public and private authority.

blocks.h2: 3. Why industries grow, consolidate or decline
paras: Growth: a new technology reduces costs or creates demand. For example, fiber optics and packet switching helped expand long-distance digital communication capacity. Consolidation: high fixed costs, acquisitions, economies of scale and network effects can reduce the number of major operators. Decline: a legacy product loses demand when a substitute is cheaper or more capable, such as dedicated consumer dial-up access being displaced by broadband. Reconfiguration: an old technology persists in a different niche; mainframes remain important in some transaction-processing environments.

Control can shift at one layer without shifting everywhere. In the Internet era, state-funded research networking expanded into privately operated access and backbone services; governments retained spectrum administration, rights-of-way, competition law, procurement and security powers. In the cloud era, companies gained extensive control over virtual compute, identity, deployment and application marketplaces; regulators responded with privacy, competition and sector-specific requirements.

A government can allocate spectrum while a private operator builds radio towers; a standards organization can specify a protocol while a cloud provider controls its implementation and billing; a bank can own a customer relationship while depending on shared payment infrastructure; an open-source project can publish source code while trademarks and hosted services remain independently controlled. To analyze power rigorously, distinguish ownership, operation, standard-setting, access policy, pricing, regulation and data governance .
References support the institutional background and technical definitions. Interpretive comparisons and illustrative models are identified as analysis rather than established causal findings.
